name: Bash
title: Bash scripting from the first echo
intro: Bash is the shell: the program that reads the commands you type in a Linux or macOS terminal. Brian Fox wrote it in 1989 for the GNU project, as a free replacement for the Bourne shell, and it is still the default on most Linux systems. A Bash script is a file of those same commands, plus variables, tests and loops to tie them together. Shell scripts start servers, build software, move files and glue other programs into pipelines. The rules feel odd at first, because everything is text and spaces matter, but they are few. Every example is a whole script and shows exactly what it prints. To run one yourself, save it as hello.sh and type bash hello.sh.

sections.p: A script usually starts with the line #!/usr/bin/env bash, which tells the system to run the file with Bash. echo prints its arguments separated by spaces and ends the line. Anything after # is a comment.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# My first script
echo Hello, squirrel!
echo "Nuts:" 42
sections.out:
Hello, squirrel!
Nuts: 42

sections.p: Set a variable with name=value, with no spaces around the =; with spaces, Bash would try to run a command called name. Read it back with $name, or ${name} when letters follow straight after. Double quotes let variables in; single quotes keep the text exactly as written.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
name=Hazel
nuts=7
echo "$name has $nuts nuts"
echo '$name has $nuts nuts'
echo "${name}s stash"
sections.out:
Hazel has 7 nuts
$name has $nuts nuts
Hazels stash

sections.p: Without quotes, Bash splits a variable's value into words at every space and squeezes runs of spaces away. Wrapping it in double quotes keeps it as one piece, exactly as stored. Quoting every "$variable" is the habit that prevents most shell bugs, especially with file names that contain spaces.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
tree="old    oak"
echo $tree
echo "$tree"
printf '[%s]\n' $tree
printf '[%s]\n' "$tree"
sections.out:
old oak
old    oak
[old]
[oak]
[old    oak]

practice.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
tree=oak
echo "Up the $tree"
echo 'Up the $tree'
options:
Up the oak
Up the oak
practice.why: Double quotes put the variable's value in. Single quotes keep the text as written.
$dayday asks for a variable called dayday, which isn't set, so it is empty. The braces mark where the name ends.

practice.q: What goes wrong with  nuts = 5  in Bash?
options: Bash tries to run a command named nuts
practice.answer: Bash tries to run a command named nuts
practice.why: With spaces, the line reads as a command (nuts) with two arguments (= and 5). Assignments must have no spaces.

sections.p: Everything in Bash is text, so 1+2 is just three characters. Arithmetic goes inside $(( ... )), where variables don't need their $. It works on whole numbers only: / drops the fraction and % gives the remainder. (( nuts++ )) changes a variable without printing anything.

if runs a command and checks whether it succeeded. [[ ... ]] is a test command: inside it, == and != compare text, and -lt, -gt, -eq compare numbers. For numbers, (( ... )) lets you write < and > as usual. The block ends with fi, which is if backwards.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
nuts=12
if (( nuts > 20 )); then
    echo feast
elif [[ $nuts -gt 10 ]]; then
    echo "good day"
else
    echo "keep looking"
fi
name=Hazel
if [[ $name == H* ]]; then
    echo "starts with H"
fi
sections.out:
good day
starts with H

sections.p: Every command finishes with an exit status: 0 means success and anything else means failure. $? holds the last command's status. && runs the next command only if the last one succeeded, and || only if it failed. This is how scripts react to errors.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
[[ 3 -lt 5 ]]
echo "status $?"
[[ 3 -gt 5 ]]
echo "status $?"
[[ -e nest.txt ]] && echo "nest found" || echo "no nest yet"
touch nest.txt
[[ -e nest.txt ]] && echo "nest found" || echo "no nest yet"
sections.out:
status 0
status 1
no nest yet
nest found

practice.why: Bash arithmetic uses whole numbers, so 7 / 2 drops the .5.
Inside [[ ]], < compares as text, and "10" sorts before "9". Inside (( )) it compares numbers, and 10 is not less than 9.

practice.q: What exit status means a command succeeded?
practice.why: There is one way to succeed and many ways to fail, so success is 0 and the other numbers name kinds of failure.

lessons.title: Loops
lessons.summary: for over lists and ranges, while, and case.

sections.p: for x in a b c runs the body once for each word. {1..5} expands to the numbers 1 to 5, and the C-style for (( i = 0; i < 3; i++ )) works too. A for over a pattern like *.txt visits matching files. The body sits between do and done.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
for tree in oak ash hazel; do
    echo "climbing $tree"
done
for n in {1..5}; do
    printf '%s ' "$n"
done
echo
for (( i = 10; i > 0; i -= 4 )); do
    printf '%s ' "$i"
done
echo
sections.out:
climbing oak
climbing ash
climbing hazel
1 2 3 4 5 
10 6 2

sections.p: while repeats as long as its command succeeds. case matches a value against patterns, each ending in ), with ;; to finish a branch and * as the catch-all. It closes with esac.
sections.out:
27
sat: nap in the drey
mon: bury nuts
wed: forage

practice.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
total=0
for n in {1..4}; do
    total=$(( total + n ))
done
echo $total
practice.why: {1..4} gives 1, 2, 3 and 4, and $(( )) adds each to the total.

options:
text: report.txt
text: photo.jpg
text: notes.txt
practice.why: case patterns work like file name patterns, so *.txt matches any name ending in .txt.

lessons.title: Arrays and expansions
lessons.summary: Indexed and associative arrays, defaults and trimming.

sections.p: An array holds a list: trees=(oak ash). trees+=(hazel) adds to it. ${trees[0]} reads one element, "${trees[@]}" gives all of them as separate words, and ${#trees[@]} counts them. The braces are required here.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
trees=(oak ash)
trees+=(hazel "silver birch")
echo "${#trees[@]} trees"
echo "first: ${trees[0]}, last: ${trees[-1]}"
for t in "${trees[@]}"; do
    echo "- $t"
done
sections.out:
4 trees
first: oak, last: silver birch
- oak
- ash
- hazel
- silver birch

sections.p: declare -A makes an associative array, which maps text keys to values. ${!stash[@]} lists the keys. Bash keeps them in no particular order, so the example pipes them through sort to print them in a fixed order.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
declare -A stash
stash[oak]=4
stash[hazel]=9
stash[oak]=$(( stash[oak] + 1 ))
for tree in $(printf '%s\n' "${!stash[@]}" | sort); do
    echo "$tree: ${stash[$tree]}"
done
sections.out:
hazel: 9
oak: 5

sections.p: Braces can also change a value as it is read. ${name:-default} gives a fallback when the variable is empty or unset. ${#name} is the length. ${file%.txt} trims a pattern from the end and ${path##*/} trims everything up to the last slash. ${name^^} makes it upper case.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
file="/home/hazel/stash.txt"
echo "${who:-nobody}"
echo "${#file}"
echo "${file##*/}"
echo "${file%.txt}.bak"
name=hazel
echo "${name^^}"
sections.out:
nobody
21
stash.txt
/home/hazel/stash.bak
HAZEL

practice.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
a=(x y z)
a+=(w)
echo "${#a[@]} ${a[1]}"
practice.why: There are four elements after the +=, and index 1 is the second one, y.
% trims the shortest match from the end (.jpg). %% trims the longest (.final.jpg).

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.summary: Arguments, local variables, return status and output.

sections.p: A function is defined with name() { ... } and called like any command. Its arguments arrive as $1, $2 and so on, $# counts them and "$@" is all of them. local keeps a variable inside the function; without it, the function would change the caller's variable of the same name.
sections.out:
Hello, Hazel (1 arguments)
Hi, Acorn (2 arguments)
count is 2

sections.p: return only sets the exit status, a number from 0 to 255, which is meant for success or failure. To hand back a real value, a function prints it and the caller captures the output with $( ... ), called command substitution.
sections.out:
3 is odd
4 is even
area is 36

practice.why: local makes a separate x that disappears when the function ends, so the outer x is untouched.
$( ) captures what the function prints instead of letting it reach the screen, so it all ends up inside the brackets.

lessons.title: Pipes, files and redirection
lessons.summary: >, >>, <, |, here-documents and small tools working together.

sections.p: > sends a command's output into a file, replacing what was there, and >> adds to the end. < feeds a file in as input. A here-document, <<EOF up to a line that says EOF, feeds the lines in between. while read takes input one line at a time.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "oak 4" > stash.txt
echo "hazel 9" >> stash.txt
cat <<EOF >> stash.txt
beech 2
ash 7
EOF
wc -l < stash.txt
while read -r tree nuts; do
    echo "$tree has $nuts"
done < stash.txt
sections.out:
4
oak has 4
hazel has 9
beech has 2
ash has 7

sections.p: | sends one command's output straight into the next command's input. Small tools, each doing one job, chain into a pipeline: tr changes characters, sort sorts lines, uniq -c counts repeated lines next to each other, and head keeps the first few. This is the Unix way of working, and Bash is the glue.
sections.out:
3 oak
      2 ash
6
15

practice.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo one > f.txt
echo two > f.txt
echo three >> f.txt
cat f.txt
practice.why: The second > replaces the file's contents, and >> then adds a line to the end.
sort puts the two a lines next to each other, uniq collapses them, and three lines are left: a, b and c.

lessons.title: Working with strings
lessons.summary: Length, slices, trimming patterns, replacing and changing case.

sections.p: Bash can cut and change the text in a variable without calling another program. ${#var} is its length and ${var:start:length} a slice. ${var#pattern} removes the shortest match from the front and ${var##pattern} the longest; % and %% do the same from the back. The patterns are the same wildcards as file names: *, ? and [abc].
sections.code:
path="/home/hazel/stash/acorns.tar.gz"
echo "length: ${#path}"
echo "first 5: ${path:0:5}"
echo "file: ${path##*/}"
echo "folder: ${path%/*}"
echo "no last extension: ${path%.*}"
echo "no extensions: ${path%%.*}"
echo "extension: ${path#*.}"
sections.out:
length: 31
first 5: /home
file: acorns.tar.gz
folder: /home/hazel/stash
no last extension: /home/hazel/stash/acorns.tar
no extensions: /home/hazel/stash/acorns
extension: tar.gz

sections.p: ${var/old/new} replaces the first match and ${var//old/new} every match. ${var^^} makes the text upper case, ${var,,} lower case, and ${var^} capitalizes the first letter.
sections.code:
line="acorn, walnut, acorn, pecan"
echo "${line/acorn/hazelnut}"
echo "${line//acorn/hazelnut}"
echo "${line//, /;}"
name="hazel"
echo "${name^} ${name^^}"
shout="STOP THAT"
echo "${shout,,}"
sections.out:
hazelnut, walnut, acorn, pecan
hazelnut, walnut, hazelnut, pecan
acorn;walnut;acorn;pecan
Hazel HAZEL
stop that

sections.p: Inside [[ ]], == compares against a wildcard pattern and =~ against a regular expression. After a regex match, the parts in parentheses are in the array BASH_REMATCH.
sections.code:
for f in notes.txt photo.JPG data.csv; do
  if [[ $f == *.txt || $f == *.csv ]]; then
    echo "$f is text"
  else
    echo "$f is something else"
  fi
done

entry="day 12: walnut x7"
if [[ $entry =~ ^day\ ([0-9]+):\ ([a-z]+)\ x([0-9]+)$ ]]; then
  echo "day=${BASH_REMATCH[1]} nut=${BASH_REMATCH[2]} count=${BASH_REMATCH[3]}"
fi
sections.out:
notes.txt is text
photo.JPG is something else
data.csv is text
day=12 nut=walnut count=7

practice.why: %.* removes the shortest .something from the end; ##*. removes everything up to the last dot.
// replaces every a, and the length of banana is 6.

practice.q: Where does Bash put the groups of a =~ match?
options: Nowhere; =~ only says yes or no
practice.why: Index 0 is the whole match and 1, 2 … are the groups.

sections.p: Every command ends with an exit status: 0 for success, anything else for failure. $? holds the last one. a && b runs b only if a succeeded, and a || b runs b only if a failed, which makes a short way to give a fallback or a message.
sections.code:
mkdir stash && echo "made stash"
mkdir stash 2>/dev/null || echo "stash already there"
false
echo "false gave $?"
true
echo "true gave $?"
grep -q acorn <<< "walnut pecan" || echo "no acorns"
[[ -d stash ]] && echo "stash is a folder"
sections.out:
made stash
stash already there
false gave 1
true gave 0
no acorns
stash is a folder

sections.p: By default a script carries on after a failed command, which can do damage. Many scripts start with set -euo pipefail: -e stops at the first failing command, -u treats an unset variable as an error, and -o pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any part of it fails, not just the last. A command tested by if, && or || doesn't stop the script.
sections.code:
set -euo pipefail

count_nuts() {
  local file=$1
  if [[ ! -f $file ]]; then
    echo "no file $file" >&2
    return 1
  fi
  wc -l < "$file"
}

printf 'acorn\nwalnut\n' > stash.txt
echo "lines: $(count_nuts stash.txt)"
if ! count_nuts missing.txt 2>/dev/null; then
  echo "handled the missing file"
fi
echo "${UNSET_THING:-default used}"
sections.out:
lines: 2
handled the missing file
default used

sections.p: trap 'commands' EXIT runs the commands when the script ends, however it ends. It's the usual way to clean up temporary files. Here the subshell in parentheses stands for a whole script: it stops at the failure, and its trap still runs.
sections.code:
(
  set -e
  tmp=$(mktemp -d)
  trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"; echo "cleaned up"' EXIT
  echo "working in a temp folder"
  touch "$tmp/nuts"
  false
  echo "never printed"
)
echo "script exit status: $?"
sections.out:
working in a temp folder
cleaned up
script exit status: 1

practice.why: false fails, so echo a is skipped, and || runs echo b.

options: A pipeline fails if any command in it fails, not only the last
Pipes are run one after another
It stops pipes from being used
practice.answer: A pipeline fails if any command in it fails, not only the last
practice.why: Without it, cmd_that_fails | sort succeeds because sort does.

practice.code:
( trap 'echo bye' EXIT; echo hi; exit 3 )
echo $?
practice.why: The trap runs as the subshell exits, and the exit status 3 is kept.

sections.p: A script's arguments are $1, $2 and so on; $# is how many there are, and "$@" is all of them, each kept whole even if it has spaces. shift drops the first one and moves the rest down. A function gets its own arguments the same way, so the example uses one to stand for a script.
sections.code:
show_args() {
  echo "$# arguments"
  for a in "$@"; do
    echo "  [$a]"
  done
  shift
  echo "after shift, first is [$1]"
}

show_args acorn "two words" pecan
sections.out:
3 arguments
  [acorn]
  [two words]
  [pecan]
after shift, first is [two words]

sections.p: getopts reads options such as -v or -n 5. The string "vn:" lists the letters it knows; a colon after a letter means it takes a value, which arrives in OPTARG. Afterwards, shift $((OPTIND - 1)) leaves only the plain arguments.
sections.out:
3 nuts counted
limit is 2, nuts are: acorn walnut pecan
2 nuts counted
usage: count_nuts [-v] [-n limit] nut...
exit status 2

options: So each argument stays one word, even if it has spaces
So the arguments are joined into one string
Quotes are needed for $@ to work at all
practice.answer: So each argument stays one word, even if it has spaces
practice.why: Unquoted, "two words" would split into two arguments.

practice.code:
f() { shift 2; echo "$# $1"; }
f a b c d
practice.why: shift 2 drops a and b, leaving c and d.

practice.q: In getopts "ab:c", which option takes a value?
practice.why: A colon after a letter means that option needs a value.

lessons.title: Project: a stash report
lessons.summary: Reading lines, matching, associative arrays and printf together.

sections.p: This script writes a small log file, then reads it line by line with while IFS= read -r. A regular expression picks out the parts of each line; lines that don't fit are reported to standard error and skipped. An associative array adds up the nuts, and printf lays out a table, sorted with sort.
sections.code:
set -euo pipefail

cat > stash.log <<'EOF'
2026-10-01 stored acorn 6
2026-10-01 stored hazelnut 2
2026-10-02 stored walnut 1
2026-10-02 ate acorn 1
oops this line is broken
2026-10-03 stored acorn 9
2026-10-03 ate hazelnut 1
EOF

declare -A total=()
stored=0 ate=0 bad=0
while IFS= read -r line; do
  if [[ $line =~ ^[0-9-]+\ (stored|ate)\ ([a-z]+)\ ([0-9]+)$ ]]; then
    action=${BASH_REMATCH[1]} nut=${BASH_REMATCH[2]} n=${BASH_REMATCH[3]}
    if [[ $action == stored ]]; then
      total[$nut]=$(( ${total[$nut]:-0} + n ))
      stored=$(( stored + n ))
    else
      total[$nut]=$(( ${total[$nut]:-0} - n ))
      ate=$(( ate + n ))
    fi
  else
    bad=$(( bad + 1 ))
  fi
done < stash.log

for nut in "${!total[@]}"; do
  printf '%-9s %3d\n' "$nut" "${total[$nut]}"
done | sort -k2,2nr -k1,1
echo "stored $stored, ate $ate, left $(( stored - ate )), unreadable lines: $bad"
sections.out:
acorn      14
hazelnut    1
walnut      1
stored 18, ate 2, left 16, unreadable lines: 1

sections.p: Take the log file's name as an argument with a -f option, print a total per day, or warn when a nut's count would go below zero.

practice.q: Why read lines with while IFS= read -r line?
options: IFS= keeps leading spaces and -r keeps backslashes, so each line arrives exactly
It splits each line into words
practice.answer: IFS= keeps leading spaces and -r keeps backslashes, so each line arrives exactly
practice.why: Without them, read trims spaces and treats backslashes as escapes.
a goes from 1 to 3, b starts from the default 0 to 5, and there are two keys.

practice.q: What does sort -k2,2nr -k1,1 do to the table?
options: Sorts by the second column as a number, largest first, then by name
Sorts by name, then by number
practice.answer: Sorts by the second column as a number, largest first, then by name
practice.why: Each -k gives a key; n is numeric and r reverses it, and the second key breaks ties.
